summary: Many peer-to-peer streaming systems use proprietary protocols. This informational document identifies the problems that causes and proposes the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol (PPSP), including a tracker protocol and a peer protocol. It discusses scope, requirements, and use cases.

plainLanguage.summary: When a video is streamed over the internet by letting the viewers pass pieces of it to each other, every such system usually has its own private way of finding other viewers and asking them for pieces. RFC 6972 argues for one common set of rules for that job, called PPSP, and then sets out what those rules have to be able to do. It is a statement of the problem and a list of requirements, not the protocol itself.

questions: why do p2p streaming systems need standards
what is a swarm in p2p streaming
how does a ppsp tracker work
subtitle: Why peer-to-peer video streaming needs a common signalling protocol, and what such a protocol must do.

tldr.problem: Almost every peer-to-peer streaming system uses its own private signalling protocol, so each new system repeats the same work and cannot easily work with content delivery networks or other operators.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol, made of a tracker protocol that hands out lists of peers and a peer protocol that exchanges the content between them, and then lists the requirements such a protocol must meet.
tldr.outcome: The document is a problem statement and a requirements list, not a protocol. It covers live and video-on-demand streaming, centralised and distributed trackers, and the security that peer-to-peer systems need because their members are strangers.

today: RFC 6972 is an Informational RFC published in July 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a problem statement and a requirements list for a peer-to-peer streaming protocol suite, and it specifies no protocol itself.

sections.title: Why One Protocol Instead of Many
sections.content:
Streaming traffic is among the largest and fastest growing traffic on the internet, and peer-to-peer streaming contributes substantially to that growth. Because it scales well and tolerates the failure of any single point, peer-to-peer streaming applications can distribute large-scale live and video-on-demand programming to a large audience with only a handful of servers. Content delivery network providers have started using peer-to-peer technology for the same reason.

As peer-to-peer streaming becomes part of the global content delivery infrastructure, the RFC argues that there is a need for an open and standard streaming signalling protocol suite. Almost all existing systems use proprietary protocols. When several proprietary protocols perform similar functions, each new system repeats work that has already been done, and the lock-in effect leads to substantial integration difficulties with other players such as content delivery networks. Enhancing existing caches to support peer-to-peer streaming is the example given: proprietary protocols can increase the complexity of interactions with different peer-to-peer applications.

The proposal is to develop an open Peer-to-Peer Streaming Protocol, abbreviated PPSP, to standardise the signalling operations in a peer-to-peer streaming system. The document states the problem and the requirements; it does not specify the protocols themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Every video streaming system that lets viewers share the video with each other has invented its own way of doing the talking. That means duplicated work and difficulty working with anyone else. The RFC asks for one common set of rules instead.

sections.title: The Words the Document Uses
sections.content:
The basic unit of data is the CHUNK, which is what peers store, schedule, advertise and exchange. Chunk size varies from several kilobytes to several megabytes in different systems. Where chunks are that large, a sub-chunk structure called a piece is often defined so that it fits in a single transmitted packet. A system may use different granularities for different purposes, for example chunks during the data exchange and a larger unit such as a set of chunks when advertising what is available.

A PEER both receives streaming content and caches and streams it to other participants. A CLIENT only receives, and a node that lacks the computing and storage to do more can act as a client; a client can be seen as a particular kind of peer. A SUPER-NODE is a special kind of peer deployed by internet service providers, more stable and with more computing power, storage and bandwidth than an ordinary peer. The SWARM is a group of peers exchanging data to distribute the chunks of the same content at a given time, identified by a swarm ID.

The TRACKER is a directory service that keeps a list of the peers taking part in a particular channel or in the distribution of a streaming file, and answers peer list queries. The tracker is a logical component, so it can be centralised or distributed, and its function may live in a dedicated server or in the peers themselves. The peer protocol handles the advertising and exchange of content, and the tracker protocol handles the initial and periodic exchange of meta-information such as peer lists.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer is a viewer that also passes the video on to other viewers. A tracker is a directory that tells viewers who else is watching the same thing. A swarm is the group of viewers sharing one particular video at one moment.

sections.title: Three Problems the Protocol Has to Solve
sections.content:
The first problem is that internet service providers meet traffic from several different peer-to-peer streaming applications, and each needs a different kind of cache. Web traffic does not have this problem, because it is made of requests and responses that any caching device can serve. Peer-to-peer traffic is produced by many applications that speak different protocols, so a provider has to deploy different types of cache for different streams, which raises both engineering and operational costs sharply.

The second is quality. Compared with client-to-server streaming, peer-to-peer streaming is often criticised for worse quality of service, with longer startup delay, longer seek delay and longer channel switch delay. A hybrid of content delivery network and peer-to-peer is the answer, but the content delivery network has to understand the specific peer-to-peer protocol in the collaboration, so proprietary protocols again raise the cost of deployment.

The third is mobile and wireless networks, which make heavy use of streaming. The RFC reports that the average volume of video traffic on mobile networks had risen to 50 per cent in the early part of 2012, and that current protocols do not transfer well to those networks. Peer-to-peer streaming assumes a stable connection with decent capacity and peers that can run for hours, which is not typical of a mobile terminal. Trackers would need more information during peer selection, such as packet loss rate, peer battery status and processing capability, and current protocols do not convey it. The frequent bitmap message, in kilobytes and exchanged every few seconds, may need to shrink. And on resource-constrained devices, several streaming applications compete for the same limited memory and disk. The RFC's suggestion is that one common client with different scheduling plug-ins is better than several clients running at once.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things make peer-to-peer streaming awkward for operators: every application needs its own kind of cache, the service is slower to start than ordinary streaming, and the protocols assume a stable broadband connection rather than a phone on a weak battery.

sections.title: Two Protocols and Five Design Challenges
sections.content:
PPSP is made of two signalling protocols: a tracker protocol between trackers and peers, and a peer protocol among the peers themselves. Between them they must let peers receive streaming content within the time constraints. The tracker protocol is best modelled as a request and response protocol carrying the information needed to select suitable peers, and its design tasks are how a peer is identified globally, how peers with different properties are distinguished, such as those with public or private addresses, those behind NAT, and those with IPv4 or IPv6 addresses, how to keep the protocol lightweight, since a tracker may serve a very large number of peers, and how the tracker can report an optimised peer list for particular content.

The peer protocol is modelled as a gossip-like protocol with periodic exchanges of neighbour and chunk-availability information. Its design tasks are how content is identified globally and verified, since content can come from anywhere and the peers must be able to tell that what they exchange is authentic, how chunk availability is identified, given the large number of chunks in a piece of content, and how to keep the protocol efficient, because the chunk availability information is exchanged frequently.

Across both protocols the RFC lists five challenges: how a peer knows which peers to contact when it joins a swarm, how it makes contact and in what manner, how to choose peers with better service capabilities and how to collect that information, how to improve communication efficiency with a compact on-the-wire message format and a suitable transport such as UDP or TCP, and how to make the system robust, for example when the tracker fails, and how to keep the tracker protocol and the peer protocol loosely coupled.
sections.plainLanguage: The design is split in two: one conversation with the directory that says who else is watching, and one conversation among the viewers themselves. The RFC then lists the awkward parts, such as how a viewer finds the right peers and how the tracker survives a failure.

sections.title: The Requirements the Protocol Must Meet
sections.content:
Four basic requirements come first. Each peer must have a unique ID, so that other peers or trackers can refer to it. The streaming content must be identified by a swarm ID, and it must be partitioned into chunks, each of which must have a unique ID within the swarm, so that a peer can tell which chunks are held by which peers and which are being asked for.

Nine operational and management requirements follow. The protocol must be configurable enough to support proxy-based and end-client setups, must have a set of configuration parameters with default values, must support diagnostic operations so that the tracker can collect peer status, and must be able to deliver a quality the streaming application can live with. That last one matters most for live streaming: the time to pick up a new channel or switch between channels should be reasonably small, and an end-to-end delay of a minute or more is not acceptable for a sporting event. Five further requirements cover remote management over a standard interface, fault monitoring of peer and server health, configuration management, performance management based on chunk distribution statistics and network load, and security management.

Four requirements cover the tracker protocol. It must let a peer ask for a peer list for a swarm, possibly tailored by the tracker, with the request carrying the peer's preferences such as how many peers it wants or how much bandwidth it prefers, and the tracker may use a traffic optimisation service such as ALTO. The protocol must report peer activity to the tracker, must take account of message frequency and bandwidth when carrying chunk availability, and must give the tracker a way to authenticate the peer. Eight requirements cover the peer protocol: it must let a peer ask other peers for chunk information, and that information must not be passed on to third parties unless it has been validated, to prevent hearsay and denial-of-service attacks. A peer must be able to ask for more peers, and the extra list must contain swarm-membership information that the receiver can verify and only peers that have been checked to be valid and online recently. Peers must report changes in chunk availability, must take account of message frequency and bandwidth, and must exchange extra information such as whether a peer is on battery or on mains power.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists four basic rules, nine rules about running and managing the system, four for talking to the tracker and eight for talking to other viewers. The running rules are the practical ones: the system must start quickly, must be diagnosable, and must not fall over when the tracker does.

sections.title: Security in a World of Strangers
sections.content:
The main security issue with this approach is that untrusted peers are used to provide the service. Malicious peers or trackers may flood the tracker with requests to cause a denial of service, originate fake information on behalf of other peers, originate fake information about chunk availability, send fake reply messages on behalf of the tracker, or leak private information about other peers or trackers.

Three security requirements answer this. The protocol must support closed swarms, where peers are authenticated or sit in a private network, so that only trusted peers can reach the original content, and it should provide mechanisms to encrypt the exchange of data among peers. It must support integrity of the streaming content, so that a peer can identify content that is not authentic. The reasoning is that in a live peer-to-peer system a polluter can introduce corrupted chunks, every receiver folds the polluted chunks it receives into its playback, and because peers forward chunks to other peers, the polluted content can spread through the network.

The third requirement is that the security mechanisms, such as key management and checksum distribution, must scale well in peer-to-peer streaming systems, where the number of participants is large and none of them is trusted in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers are strangers, so the protocol has to assume some of them are lying or attacking. It must allow a closed group where members are known, must let viewers spot damaged video, and must keep its security machinery cheap enough to run across thousands of viewers.

viz.caption: THE FIVE CHALLENGES FOR THE PROTOCOL DESIGNERS

items.title: Finding peers
items.text: When a peer joins a swarm, how does it learn which peers to contact?

items.title: Making contact
items.text: After choosing a set of peers, how does a peer reach them, and in what manner?

items.title: Choosing good peers
items.text: How to pick peers with better service, and how to collect that information.

items.title: Efficiency
items.text: A compact message format and a suitable transport, UDP or TCP.

items.title: Robustness
items.text: What happens when the tracker fails, and how to keep the two protocols loosely coupled.

viz.caption: THE REQUIREMENT GROUPS AND HOW MANY EACH HOLDS

cells: Peer ID, swarm ID, chunking and chunk ID
Configuration, diagnostics, quality, management and fault monitoring
Peer lists, activity reporting, efficiency and peer authentication
Chunk information, peer lists, availability updates and extra peer status
Closed swarms, content integrity and scalable security mechanisms

viz.caption: WHAT A MALICIOUS PEER OR TRACKER MAY DO

items.title: Flood the tracker
items.text: Send a large number of requests so the tracker cannot serve others.

items.title: Forge other peers
items.text: Originate fake information on behalf of peers that did not send it.

items.title: Fake chunk availability
items.text: Claim to hold content that does not exist.

items.title: Forge the tracker
items.text: Send reply messages that look as if they came from the tracker.

items.title: Leak information
items.text: Reveal private information about other peers or trackers.
